items.stem: A company runs an internet-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances reach the internet through NAT gateways. The operations team is small and does not write its own detection rules. Attackers send requests that contain SQL injection code to the application. The company must block these requests. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: requests that contain SQL injection code
does not write its own detection rules

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: A web ACL on the load balancer reads each request, and the SQL database rule group blocks request patterns [like SQL injection attacks](../facts/waf.md#waf-sql-database-group).

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group, and route the private subnets' traffic through the firewall endpoints.
options.why: A domain list rule group looks for domain names in the [Server Name Indication (SNI) extension](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-sni-host-header) or the host header, so it does not read SQL injection code.
options.misconception: believes that a domain list rule group reads the content of requests that arrive at a load balancer

options.text: Add security group rules and network ACL rules that inspect the domain names and the content of the traffic.
options.why: Security groups and network ACLs give [traffic control at a Layer 4 level (IP address and port ranges)](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-sec05-finer-control-services), so they do not read request content.

options.text: Run proxy software on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that inspects every inbound request and every outbound connection.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds, patches and scales a proxy fleet and writes its rules, which is far more work than a managed rule group.

items.explanation: SQL injection code arrives inside HTTP requests, so the control reads each request at the load balancer. AWS and AWS Marketplace sellers [automatically update managed rule groups](../facts/waf.md#waf-managed-rules-auto-updated) when new threats emerge, so the small team writes no rules and runs no extra instances.
items.takeaway: Attack code inside web requests: a web ACL with managed rule groups on the load balancer.
items.twin: If the stem said "The instances must reach only an approved list of software update domains" instead: AWS Network Firewall, because it supports [allow lists and deny lists with domain names](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-allow-deny-lists).
items.say: Attack code is inside the request, so I'd put a web ACL with managed rules on the load balancer.

solvers.stem_only: Block SQL injection at layer 7 with no self-written rules: associate an AWS WAF web ACL with AWS managed rule groups (SQL database / core rule set) with the Application Load Balancer.

items.stem: A company serves a login page through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of an Application Load Balancer. Each minute, the page receives thousands of requests from a small set of IP addresses. The set of addresses changes every few hours. Real users send a few requests each. The company must stop the flood as soon as possible without blocking real users. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: a small set of IP addresses

options.text: Add network ACL deny rules for the attacking IP addresses to the load balancer subnets, and update the rules when the addresses change.
options.why: The addresses change every few hours, so someone edits the rules by hand, and a network ACL has [20 rules per network ACL](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-quota-rules-per-network-acl) by default.

options.text: Add a rate-based rule to a web ACL on the CloudFront distribution that blocks each IP address above a request limit.
options.why: On CloudFront, blocked requests are [stopped before they reach your web servers](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-rules-run-at-edge), and the rule needs no address list.

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and ask the Shield Response Team to block the attacking IP addresses during each attack.
options.why: It can help, but Shield Advanced needs a [1-year subscription commitment](../facts/shield.md#shield-advanced-one-year-commitment) and a monthly fee, which costs far more than one rate-based rule.

options.text: Add inbound deny rules for the attacking IP addresses to the security group of the load balancer, and update them when the addresses change.
options.why: In a security group, [you can specify allow rules, but not deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only), so the deny list does not exist.

items.explanation: A few addresses send many requests, which is the case that rate-based rules handle: AWS designs them for [brute force login attempts](../facts/waf.md#waf-faq-rate-based-web-layer-ddos). After an address passes the limit, its new requests are blocked until [the request rate falls below the configured threshold](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls). The rule follows the changing addresses by itself, and real users stay under the limit.
items.takeaway: A few addresses that send too many requests: a rate-based rule in the web ACL.
items.twin: If the stem said "thousands of IP addresses that each try a few stolen passwords" instead: a per-address limit misses them, so add the account takeover prevention rule group, which works by [inspecting login attempts](../facts/waf.md#waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts).
items.say: A few addresses send too much, so a rate-based rule blocks each one until it slows down.

solvers.stem_only: Per-IP flood from changing addresses while real users send few requests: an AWS WAF rate-based rule on a web ACL associated with the CloudFront distribution, which blocks each IP above a limit automatically and needs no IP list maintenance.

items.stem: A company protects its sign-in page with an AWS WAF web ACL on an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The sign-in page is part of the company's own web application. The web ACL has a rate-based rule that limits each IP address. Attackers now try stolen user names and passwords from thousands of IP addresses, and each address sends a few requests each hour. Real users must keep signing in during the attack. The company must ensure that requests with stolen credentials are stopped. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Real users must keep signing in

options.text: Lower the request limit of the existing rate-based rule so that each IP address can send fewer sign-in requests.
options.why: The rule counts each address separately, [based on the request IP address](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-default-key-ip), and each attacking address stays far below a limit that real users can reach.

options.text: Add a rate-based rule with a scope-down statement for the sign-in page that counts all requests and blocks them above a limit.
options.why: [A rate-based rule with a scope-down statement](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-scope-down) and Count all limits the sign-in requests together, so real users are blocked too when the total passes the limit.
options.misconception: believes that a limit on all sign-in requests blocks the attackers and not the real users

options.text: Export the AWS WAF logs each day, build an IP set of the addresses that failed to sign in, and block that IP set.
options.why: A daily IP set is a day behind thousands of changing addresses, and the team rebuilds the set by hand each day.
options.misconception: believes that a daily block list keeps up with an attack from thousands of addresses

options.text: Add the AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention managed rule group to the web ACL, and point it at the sign-in endpoint.
options.why: The rule group monitors the login page to [detect unauthorized access to user accounts](../facts/waf.md#waf-faq-atp-login-page) that uses compromised credentials.

items.explanation: Each address stays below a per-address limit, so request counting misses the attack. The account takeover prevention (ATP) managed rule group works by [inspecting login attempts](../facts/waf.md#waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts) and checks them [against its stolen credential database](../facts/waf.md#waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts). It acts on the credentials, not on the request rate, so real users keep signing in.
items.takeaway: Stolen passwords from many addresses: the ATP managed rule group, not a lower per-address limit.
items.twin: If the stem said "from a few IP addresses that each send thousands of requests" instead: the existing rate-based rule works, because new requests stay blocked until [the request rate falls below the configured threshold](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls).

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead, and the sentence before it asks me to ensure that requests with stolen credentials are stopped.
I mark the constraints: stolen user names and passwords, thousands of IP addresses, a few requests from each address, and real users must keep signing in.
Before I look at the options, I predict a managed rule group that checks the credentials themselves, because each address stays under a per-address limit.

I remove the lower limit on the existing rule, because the rule counts each IP address on its own and every attacking address stays far below it. I remove the daily IP set, because it is a day late and the team rebuilds it by hand.

Between the scope-down rule with Count all and the account takeover prevention rule group the difference is who gets blocked; the stem says real users must keep signing in, so a limit on all sign-in requests fails when the attack pushes the total above it.
Check: the account takeover prevention rule group inspects login attempts, compares them with a stolen credential database, and needs no list from the team. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Low-and-slow credential stuffing from many IPs defeats per-IP rate limits; use the AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention (ATP) managed rule group on the login endpoint, which checks submitted credentials against stolen-credential data and failed-login patterns.

items.stem: A small company serves its public website through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The company is worried about SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks against the website. The company has never subscribed to any AWS Shield plan and has not created any AWS WAF web ACL. The company requires protection against these attacks without a new subscription or new configuration. Which service meets these requirements?
keywords: SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks
without a new subscription or new configuration

options.text: AWS Shield Standard, which is already active for the distribution
options.why: [All AWS customers benefit from the automatic protection](../facts/shield.md#shield-standard-automatic-no-charge) of Shield Standard, so the distribution is protected now.

options.text: AWS Shield Advanced, after the company subscribes and adds the distribution
options.why: Shield Advanced [provides expanded DDoS attack protection](../facts/shield.md#shield-advanced-paid-expanded-protection) for a fee; the basic protection against these floods is already active without it.

options.text: AWS WAF, after a web ACL with a rate-based rule is associated
options.why: AWS WAF inspects at the [request-level](../facts/waf.md#waf-vs-shield-inspection-level), and AWS Shield inspects these floods at the [packet-level](../facts/waf.md#waf-vs-shield-inspection-level).

options.text: AWS Network Firewall, after a firewall is deployed in the origin VPC
options.why: Network Firewall is designed to control access to and from a VPC, [but not to mitigate volumetric attacks](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-not-for-ddos) such as these floods.

items.explanation: SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks are infrastructure events at [layer 3 and 4](../facts/shield.md#shield-faq-standard-layer-3-4-all-customers). AWS Shield Standard protects against them [for all AWS customers](../facts/shield.md#shield-faq-standard-layer-3-4-all-customers), and customers get it [at no additional charge](../facts/shield.md#shield-standard-automatic-no-charge). No subscription and no web ACL are needed.
items.takeaway: SYN and UDP floods: Shield Standard already protects every AWS account, with no subscription.
items.twin: If the stem said "SQL injection attempts against the website" instead: AWS WAF with a managed rule group, because AWS WAF [protects against exploits on web applications](../facts/waf.md#waf-vs-shield-primary-purpose).
items.say: Shield Standard is already on for every account, so the SYN floods are covered today.

solvers.stem_only: Layer 3/4 attacks such as SYN floods and UDP reflection, with no new subscription or configuration: AWS Shield Standard, which is automatic and free for CloudFront.

items.stem: A company runs a mission-critical web application behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution and an Application Load Balancer. The company has an AWS Enterprise Support plan. During a DDoS attack, the company must get help from AWS DDoS experts at any hour. The company also must be able to request a credit for the scaling charges that an attack causes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: help from AWS DDoS experts at any hour
request a credit for the scaling charges

options.text: Rely on AWS Shield Standard, and open an AWS Support case to request DDoS help and a billing refund during each attack.
options.why: The response team and cost protection come with Shield Advanced, which adds [24/7 support from the Shield Response Team](../facts/shield.md#shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection); Shield Standard is the automatic basic layer.
options.misconception: believes that Shield Standard includes the Shield Response Team and cost protection credits

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and add the distribution and the load balancer as protected resources after an attack starts.
options.why: Resources [added during an attack are not eligible](../facts/shield.md#shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack) for a credit, so the company loses cost protection for the attack that is already running.
options.misconception: believes that protection added during an attack still qualifies for a credit

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced now, and protect both resources, each with a web ACL that has a rate-based rule in Block mode.
options.why: The response team serves Shield Advanced subscribers on the [Business Support plan](../facts/shield.md#shield-srt-needs-business-or-enterprise-support) or Enterprise Support, and early protection with a Block rule keeps the credit eligible.

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced now, protect both resources with rate-based rules, and place AWS Network Firewall endpoints in front of the load balancer.
options.why: The Shield part works, but the endpoints add work, and Network Firewall is designed for VPC access control, [but not to mitigate volumetric attacks](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-not-for-ddos).

items.explanation: Shield Advanced adds [24/7 support from the Shield Response Team](../facts/shield.md#shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection), and after an attack you can [request a Shield Advanced service credit](../facts/shield.md#shield-cost-protection-credit) for the extra charges. Resources [added during an attack are not eligible](../facts/shield.md#shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack), so both resources are protected now, each with a rate-based rule [in the web ACL in Block mode](../facts/shield.md#shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack).
items.takeaway: DDoS experts and cost credits: Shield Advanced, with protection and a Block rate rule in place before the attack.
items.twin: If the stem said "must keep costs low and needs no DDoS experts" instead: Shield Standard with AWS WAF rate-based rules, because Shield Standard comes [at no additional charge](../facts/shield.md#shield-standard-automatic-no-charge).

solvers.stem_only: 24/7 access to the Shield Response Team (needs Business or Enterprise Support) and cost protection credits: subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced now and add CloudFront and the ALB as protected resources before an attack, with an AWS WAF web ACL that has a rate-based rule (needed for layer 7 cost protection eligibility).

items.stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and adds new member accounts every month. The accounts run Application Load Balancers in two AWS Regions and Amazon CloudFront distributions. The security team must centrally manage one set of AWS WAF rules for every load balancer and every distribution, including the resources in new accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: adds new member accounts every month

options.text: Write a script that runs each day in every account, creates a web ACL in each Region, and associates it with each new resource.
options.why: It can work, but the team maintains a script in every account and Region, which is more work than one managed policy.

options.text: Turn on AWS Firewall Manager separately in each account, and create one AWS WAF policy in each account that covers all Regions.
options.why: Firewall Manager runs from [the Firewall Manager administrator account](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-faq-prereq-administrator-account), and [security policies are region specific](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-policies-region-specific), so one policy does not cover all Regions.
options.misconception: believes that Firewall Manager runs in each account without an administrator account and that one policy covers all Regions

options.text: Subscribe the organization to AWS Shield Advanced so that AWS applies web exploit rules to the resources in every account automatically.
options.why: Shield Advanced is DDoS protection, and AWS Shield [does not inspect the contents](../facts/shield.md#shield-no-http-content-inspection) of HTTP requests, so it adds no web exploit rules.

options.text: Enable AWS Config, set a Firewall Manager administrator account, and create a Global AWS WAF policy plus one per Region with load balancers.
options.why: This is the Firewall Manager setup: the administrator account owns the policies, and new accounts in scope receive them with no extra step.

items.explanation: Firewall Manager lets you [centrally configure and manage firewall rules](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-definition-central-rules) across the organization, and in a new account [Firewall Manager automatically applies the policy](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-auto-applies-to-new-accounts). It also needs AWS Config: [you must enable AWS Config](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-requires-aws-config). CloudFront distributions use one Global policy, and load balancers need [separate Firewall Manager policies for each Region](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-waf-policy-global-for-cloudfront).
items.takeaway: The same AWS WAF rules in every account, new ones too: Firewall Manager AWS WAF policies.
items.twin: If the stem said "one account with one load balancer" instead: associate one web ACL with the load balancer directly, because Firewall Manager suits cases where you [protect your entire organization](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-best-for-whole-org).
items.say: For many accounts I'd use Firewall Manager, so new accounts get the same web ACL rules automatically.

solvers.stem_only: Central AWS WAF rules across an organization including new accounts: AWS Firewall Manager with an administrator account (prerequisites Organizations all features and AWS Config), one global WAF policy for CloudFront and one regional policy per Region for the ALBs, with auto remediation.

items.stem: A company's developers work in the Europe (Ireland) Region. A developer creates an AWS WAF web ACL and an IP set in Europe (Ireland) to block a list of addresses. The web ACL must protect an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin of the distribution is an Application Load Balancer in US West (Oregon). When the developer tries to associate the web ACL, the distribution does not appear in the list of resources. What should the developer do?

options.text: Create the web ACL and the IP set again in US East (N. Virginia), and associate the web ACL with the distribution.
options.why: A web ACL for CloudFront and the resources it uses [use the Region US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1), and there the distribution appears in the list.

options.text: Associate the IP set directly with the distribution, and keep the web ACL in Europe (Ireland) for later use.
options.why: In a rule, [you reference the set](../facts/waf.md#waf-ip-set-collection-of-addresses) through an IP set statement; an IP set is not associated with a resource on its own.
options.misconception: believes that an IP set attaches to a resource without a web ACL

options.text: Create the web ACL and the IP set again in US West (Oregon), the origin's Region, and associate the web ACL there.
options.why: The origin's Region does not decide it: a web ACL goes in [the Region where the associated resource is located](../facts/waf.md#waf-web-acl-region-of-resource), and for a distribution that is [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/waf.md#waf-web-acl-region-of-resource).
options.misconception: believes that a CloudFront web ACL follows the Region of the origin

options.text: Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the distribution first, so that the distribution appears in the list of web ACL resources.
options.why: Shield Advanced is DDoS protection and does not change where a web ACL for CloudFront is created; AWS WAF is [available globally for CloudFront distributions](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1).

items.explanation: AWS WAF is [available globally for CloudFront distributions](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1), but you [use the Region US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1) to create the web ACL and the resources that it uses. An IP set for such a web ACL is created in the Global scope as well: [you must use Global (CloudFront)](../facts/waf.md#waf-ip-set-global-for-cloudfront).
items.takeaway: A web ACL for CloudFront and its IP sets are created in US East (N. Virginia), whatever the origin Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "must protect the Application Load Balancer" instead: create the web ACL in US West (Oregon), [the Region where the associated resource is located](../facts/waf.md#waf-web-acl-region-of-resource).

solvers.stem_only: Web ACLs for CloudFront are global (CLOUDFRONT scope) and are created in US East (N. Virginia); recreate the web ACL and IP set there (IP sets are scoped the same way) and associate it with the distribution.

items.stem: A company runs workloads in private subnets across multiple Availability Zones of one VPC. The VPC has public subnets and a NAT gateway in each of its three zones. All traffic between the internet and the workloads must be inspected by AWS Network Firewall. The inspection must continue if one Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST resilient way? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a dedicated firewall subnet in each Availability Zone, and place one firewall endpoint in each of these subnets.
options.why: Each zone gets [a subnet to host the primary firewall endpoint](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoints-per-az), so a zone failure removes one endpoint and the other zones keep their inspection.

options.text: Create one firewall endpoint in a single Availability Zone, and route the traffic of all three zones through that endpoint.
options.why: It inspects the traffic, but one endpoint in one zone is a single point of failure for all three zones, which is the least resilient design.
options.misconception: believes that one firewall endpoint serves every zone with the same resilience

options.text: Place the firewall endpoints in the same subnets as the workloads, so that no extra subnets are needed in the VPC.
options.why: An endpoint protects subnets [except for the one in which it's located](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoint-not-own-subnet), so workloads in its own subnet are not inspected.
options.misconception: believes that a firewall endpoint can share a subnet with the workloads that it protects

options.text: Update the route tables so that the traffic of each zone goes in both directions through the firewall endpoint in that same zone.
options.why: Same-zone routing sends each flow through [the Network Firewall endpoint in both directions](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-no-asymmetric-routing), and a zone failure leaves the routes of the other zones intact.

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the internet gateway, and add rule groups that inspect all inbound and outbound packets.
options.why: A web ACL protects resources such as [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer](../facts/waf.md#waf-protected-resource-types); an internet gateway is not in that list.

items.explanation: Firewall endpoints are installed [on a per-Availability Zone basis](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoints-per-az), each in [a dedicated subnet](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-faq-dedicated-subnet-28). Incoming traffic goes to [the firewall in the same Availability Zone](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-two-az-same-zone-routing) as its subnet, so one zone failure stops one endpoint, not all inspection.
items.takeaway: Network Firewall across zones: one endpoint in a dedicated subnet per zone, and same-zone routes both ways.
items.twin: If the stem said "in one Availability Zone" instead: one firewall subnet and one endpoint are enough, because endpoints are installed [on a per-Availability Zone basis](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoints-per-az).

solvers.stem_only: Create a dedicated firewall subnet with one Network Firewall endpoint in each Availability Zone, and route each zone's traffic symmetrically (both directions) through its same-zone endpoint, so one zone failure does not stop inspection elsewhere.

items.stem: A company runs a website behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution and an Application Load Balancer. An HTTP GET flood from many IP addresses slows down the website. Many of these addresses are already associated with bots. The company has AWS Shield Standard and no other AWS protection service. Which combination of steps will protect the website against such floods in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: HTTP GET flood from many IP addresses

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and add the CloudFront distribution and the load balancer as protected resources.
options.why: It can help, but Shield Advanced needs a [1-year subscription commitment](../facts/shield.md#shield-advanced-one-year-commitment) and a monthly fee; two AWS WAF rules stop this flood without a subscription.

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the distribution, and add a rate-based rule that blocks IP addresses above a request limit.
options.why: A rate-based rule blocks each address until [the request rate falls below the configured threshold](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls), which stops the flood at the edge.

options.text: Add network ACL deny rules for the flooding IP addresses to the subnets of the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: The flood comes from many addresses, and a network ACL has [20 rules per network ACL](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-quota-rules-per-network-acl) by default, so the deny list does not fit.

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in the VPC, and add stateful rules that drop inbound HTTP traffic from the flooding addresses.
options.why: Network Firewall is designed to control VPC access, [but not to mitigate volumetric attacks](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-not-for-ddos) such as this flood.

options.text: Add the Amazon IP reputation list managed rule group to an AWS WAF web ACL that protects the distribution.
options.why: The rule group blocks addresses [typically associated with bots or other threats](../facts/waf.md#waf-ip-reputation-list-group), including bot addresses that stay under the rate limit.

items.explanation: AWS WAF rate-based rules are designed for [web-layer DDoS attacks](../facts/waf.md#waf-faq-rate-based-web-layer-ddos), and on CloudFront blocked requests are [stopped before they reach your web servers](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-rules-run-at-edge). The Amazon IP reputation list is [based on Amazon internal threat intelligence](../facts/waf.md#waf-ip-reputation-list-group). Both rules run in one web ACL, with no subscription.
items.takeaway: A web-layer flood on a budget: a rate-based rule and the IP reputation list in one web ACL.
items.twin: If the stem said "must get help from AWS DDoS experts during attacks" instead: add AWS Shield Advanced, because it includes [24/7 support from the Shield Response Team](../facts/shield.md#shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection).

solvers.stem_only: Use AWS WAF at the edge, not Shield Advanced (too costly for a layer 7 flood that WAF handles): associate a WAF web ACL with the CloudFront distribution, add a rate-based rule that blocks source IPs exceeding a request threshold, and add the AWS managed Amazon IP reputation list rule group to block known bot IP addresses. Network ACLs and Network Firewall act inside the VPC behind CloudFront and cannot see the client IPs well or scale for many changing addresses.

items.stem: A company has many AWS accounts in AWS Organizations with all features enabled. AWS Config is enabled in every account. A review finds security groups that allow SSH on port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. From a single location, the security team must audit the security group rules in every account, including new accounts, and must fix such rules automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS WAF web ACL in every account with a rule that blocks port 22, and associate it with each EC2 instance.
options.why: A web ACL protects resources such as [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer](../facts/waf.md#waf-protected-resource-types); an EC2 instance is not in that list, and a web ACL does not change security group rules.

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in each VPC with a stateless rule that drops traffic to port 22 from any address.
options.why: Network Firewall filters the traffic that route tables send [through the Network Firewall firewall endpoints](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-route-tables-enable-protection), and the open security group rules stay in place.
options.misconception: believes that dropping traffic in the network fixes the open security group rules

options.text: Create an AWS Firewall Manager security group policy that checks rule content and remediates noncompliant rules, scoped to the organization.
options.why: One policy from the administrator account covers the organization, and automatic remediation fixes the open rules with no manual step.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function in each account that scans security groups each hour and deletes rules that allow SSH from any address.
options.why: It can work, but the team writes, deploys and maintains code in every account, including each new account, which a managed policy avoids.

items.explanation: A Firewall Manager security group policy can [Audit security group rules](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-sg-policy-three-uses) to find and fix noncompliant rules, and a policy can [automatically remediate noncompliant resources](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-audit-or-auto-remediate). In a new account, [Firewall Manager automatically applies the policy](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-auto-applies-to-new-accounts), so the team writes no code for each account.
items.takeaway: Find and fix risky security group rules in every account: a Firewall Manager security group policy.
items.twin: If the stem said "must report the open rules without changing them" instead: the same policy type that lists noncompliant resources [without taking corrective action](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-audit-or-auto-remediate).

solvers.stem_only: Organization-wide audit and auto-remediation of overly permissive security group rules from one place: AWS Firewall Manager security group content audit policy with auto remediation, scoped to the organization.

items.stem: A company serves a web application from Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets across two Availability Zones. A Network Load Balancer receives the HTTP requests from users on the internet and forwards them to the instances. The security team must block common web exploits, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: A Network Load Balancer receives the HTTP requests

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups directly with the existing Network Load Balancer.
options.why: The list of resources that a web ACL protects names [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer](../facts/waf.md#waf-protected-resource-types) and others, and it does not name a Network Load Balancer.

options.text: Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and add the Elastic IP addresses of the Network Load Balancer as protected resources.
options.why: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS floods, but AWS Shield [does not inspect the contents](../facts/shield.md#shield-no-http-content-inspection) of HTTP requests, so SQL injection code passes.

options.text: Move the traffic to an Application Load Balancer, and associate a web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with it.
options.why: On an Application Load Balancer, [your rules run in region](../facts/waf.md#waf-regional-rules-run-in-region-internal), and the managed rule groups block common exploits without rules that the team writes.

options.text: Install an open source web application firewall on each EC2 instance, and update its detection rules from a public feed every week.
options.why: It can work, but the team installs, patches and updates software on every instance, which is far more work than a managed web ACL.

items.explanation: AWS WAF reads web requests on regional services such as an Application Load Balancer, where [your rules run in region](../facts/waf.md#waf-regional-rules-run-in-region-internal). The list of resource types for a web ACL does not name a Network Load Balancer, so the traffic moves to an Application Load Balancer. Managed rule groups are rules that [AWS and AWS Marketplace sellers write and maintain](../facts/waf.md#waf-managed-rule-groups-definition), and the core rule set is [generally applicable to web applications](../facts/waf.md#waf-core-rule-set-owasp).
items.takeaway: A web ACL protects an Application Load Balancer; its list of resource types does not name a Network Load Balancer.
items.twin: If the stem said "behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution" instead: associate the web ACL with the distribution, because AWS WAF is [available globally for CloudFront distributions](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1).
items.say: AWS WAF doesn't sit on a Network Load Balancer, so I'd move the traffic to an Application Load Balancer with a web ACL.

solvers.stem_only: AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer; put an Application Load Balancer (or CloudFront) in front and associate a web ACL with AWS managed rule groups for SQL injection and XSS.

items.stem: A company runs an internet-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances reach the internet through NAT gateways. The operations team is small and does not write its own detection rules. A review finds that the instances can download files from any domain on the internet. The instances must reach only an approved list of software update domains. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: download files from any domain on the internet
an approved list of software update domains

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: A web ACL on the load balancer reads requests that arrive at the load balancer; the instances' outbound connections leave through the NAT gateways and do not pass the web ACL.
options.misconception: believes that a web ACL on the load balancer filters the outbound traffic of the instances

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group, and route the private subnets' traffic through the firewall endpoints.
options.why: The rule group holds the approved update domains as an allow list, and the route tables send the instances' traffic [through the Network Firewall firewall endpoints](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-route-tables-enable-protection).

options.text: Add security group rules and network ACL rules that inspect the domain names and the content of the traffic.
options.why: Security groups and network ACLs give [traffic control at a Layer 4 level (IP address and port ranges)](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-sec05-finer-control-services), so they do not read domain names.

options.text: Run proxy software on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that inspects every inbound request and every outbound connection.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds, patches and scales a proxy fleet and writes its rules, which is far more work than a managed firewall.

items.explanation: The outbound connections leave the VPC, so the control sits in their route. Network Firewall supports [allow lists and deny lists with domain names](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-allow-deny-lists), and for HTTPS it reads the [Server Name Indication (SNI) extension](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-sni-host-header). Protection starts after [you modify your Amazon VPC route tables](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-route-tables-enable-protection) so that the private subnets' traffic goes through the firewall endpoints.
items.takeaway: Outbound traffic to approved domains: Network Firewall with a domain list, in the route of the traffic.
items.twin: If the stem said "Attackers send requests that contain SQL injection code to the application" instead: a web ACL with managed rule groups, because they block patterns [like SQL injection attacks](../facts/waf.md#waf-sql-database-group).
items.say: Outbound domain filtering is a Network Firewall job, with the route tables sending the traffic through it.

solvers.stem_only: Egress domain allow-listing for instances in private subnets: AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group (allow list), with routes from the private subnets through the firewall endpoints to the NAT gateways.
